body_markdown:
## Deals Stall Even With Good Counsel


Consider a common situation. A customer returned a marked-up order form nine days ago. The sales team wants to know when the order form will go out, and the founder wants to know where the redline stands. Nobody knows, because the order form is with an outside firm that nobody has been in touch with recently. The firm's last work product was a memo that identified eleven risks without recommending a course of action.


Each participant did their job. The company retained capable counsel, and counsel gave accurate advice. However, the deal remains stalled because counsel is too far removed from the business to resolve the holdup.


As a forward-deployed attorney at General Legal, I function effectively as a member of client companies, in their Slack workspaces and on their deal desks, reviewing the same transactions their sales leaders do each week. The term for this model, borrowed from software engineering, is 'forward-deployed,' because no conventional terms for legal services capture this way of working.


## The Term's Origin


The term 'forward-deployed' originated at Palantir. Rather than ship its software and leave customers to implement it, Palantir placed engineers at customer sites. Those engineers learned the customer's domain, such as fraud detection at a bank or parts flow at a manufacturer, and built on the platform to address their specific problems.


Other companies have since adopted the model. OpenAI has a forward-deployed engineering team that hires in cities from San Francisco to Tokyo, and Ramp organizes its forward-deployed engineers in pods. Google Cloud is hiring forward-deployed engineers in several countries, and in June 2026, AWS announced a $1 billion forward-deployed engineering organization. Each case uses the same underlying premise that a product delivers value best when someone who understands both the technology and the customer's workflows connects the two.


Law firms have faced the same distance from their clients' work for much longer. Typically, they describe it as 'scope,' the boundary that determines which questions outside counsel will answer as part of existing work and which must wait for a new matter.


## The Job of a Forward-Deployed Attorney


A forward-deployed attorney works in the client's Slack rather than through email. An email to outside counsel typically becomes a matter, with a kickoff call, a scoping email, and a billing number. A question in a shared channel can be answered within minutes by an attorney who already knows the relevant history, such as which customer's security team ended negotiations in June.


Over time, the attorney makes an impact on other aspects of the organization, and the legal questions change. In the first month, a sales representative may ask whether they can agree to a term. By the third month, the same representative asks which approved fallback position to use. The forward-deployed attorney helps to create a system that the team is able to apply more independently, ultimately leading to a more efficient business function.


A key aspect of working as a forward-deployed attorney is being proactive. Before features ship, I review the product roadmap to ensure the data processing agreement lists any new subprocessor, so that a customer's privacy team does not discover an omission. I monitor the deal desk so that when one clause repeatedly stalls deals, I can revise the template instead of renegotiating the clause in each negotiation. Because I understand that handoffs between teams are a common source of delays, I manage the contract process from intake through signature, including the obligations that continue after signing.


Proximity to clients allows forward-deployed attorneys to provide legal insight while business decisions are still open.


## A Fixed-Fee Arrangement


As someone who has billed by the hour, I believe hourly billing discourages the work that makes companies faster. Forward deployment asks a lawyer to spend what would be unbilled time reading product specifications that fall outside any open matter. It calls for playbooks that will eliminate many of the questions the lawyer is currently paid to answer. It also requires the lawyer to be available for questions too brief to justify opening a file. Under an hourly arrangement, each of these might be a write-off on the final bill. The lawyer who answers questions as a favor or looks deeply into client materials to prepare for potential future matters appears least productive when it comes to the billable-hour targets that firms use to measure performance.


Fixed fees address this problem. When a matter is priced as a deliverable, every hour saved benefits the lawyer instead of reducing the fee, which creates a reason to build the playbooks and templates that save those hours. This is one reason forward deployment and fixed pricing tend to go together, and, in our view, neither works well without the other.


## Best Fit for Forward Deployment


Large companies solved the problem of distance by bringing lawyers in-house. They hired a general counsel, additional lawyers, and a contracts manager, and the general counsel joined the leadership team's regular meetings. Forward deployment gives companies a similar arrangement before they can support that headcount.


Forward-deployed attorneys work best for companies with three characteristics. First, they ship products quickly, so their contracts must keep pace with product changes. Second, their contracts repeat, with the same order form, the same data processing agreement, and the same recurring objections from customer procurement teams, so a playbook can be reused across many deals. Third, most of their legal questions call for commercial judgment rather than specialized litigation or cross-border tax planning.


For example, an AI company at the Series A stage typically fits this profile. A change to the model can necessitate a cascade of changes to the customer-facing AI terms, the data processing agreement, the subprocessor list, and the answers in a security questionnaire for a live deal. These documents are closely linked, meaning the job of keeping them consistent must be done by someone who understands how they connect.


The forward deployment model is not suited to every type of work. Examples include bet-the-company litigation, novel regulatory disputes, and initial public offerings. Forward deployment is apt for the operating layer of a business, where many small decisions each year together set the company's pace.


## Should You Hire a Forward-Deployed Attorney?


The following three questions may be instructive for company leadership in assessing whether their legal function keeps pace with the business:


1. How long does a standard customer agreement take from first redline to signature? (Does anyone track this timeline?)
2. When a sales representative encounters an unfamiliar term, is there a written answer they can find without opening a ticket?
3. After a product change, how long does it take for contracts and the privacy policy to reflect it?


If no one tracks turnaround time, no written guidance exists, and contracts lag behind the product, hiring higher-quality counsel may not move the needle. This is because the core problem is that your legal function is too distant from the company. Even highly responsive outside counsel remain outside the company.


General Legal addresses this with forward-deployed attorneys who work inside the companies we serve. Each client has a named attorney in its Slack workspace who knows the product roadmap, scopes and prices matters in advance, and creates templates and playbooks that give client teams easy access to the answers for routine legal questions.


Forward-deployed counsel who works inside the business empowers companies to move at their own pace without compromising on legal protection.


Key takeaways


- •


Forward-deployed attorneys work inside client companies' daily operations—in Slack channels, on deal desks, and alongside product teams—rather than being retained for discrete matters from outside.


- •


The model originated in software engineering at Palantir, where engineers were embedded at customer sites to understand their specific workflows and build tailored solutions.


- •


Fixed-fee pricing enables forward deployment by removing the disincentive hourly billing creates for proactive work like building playbooks and monitoring product roadmaps.


- •


This approach works best for companies that ship products quickly, have repeating contract patterns, and need commercial judgment rather than specialized litigation or complex regulatory work.


- •


Forward-deployed attorneys identify issues proactively—such as outdated subprocessor lists or contract clauses that repeatedly stall deals—before they become problems in live transactions.


TL;DR


Core Definition A lawyer embedded in a company's operations—Slack, deal desk, product roadmap—who identifies issues proactively and builds reusable systems rather than answering one-off questions.


Origin of the Model Borrowed from Palantir's practice of placing engineers at customer sites; now used by OpenAI, Ramp, Google Cloud, and AWS to connect product expertise with customer workflows.


How It Works Attorney works in client Slack channels, reviews product roadmaps before features ship, monitors deal desk to revise stalling clauses, and manages contracts from intake through signature.


Pricing Structure Fixed fees align incentives by rewarding efficiency—lawyers benefit from creating playbooks and templates that save time rather than billing hourly for repetitive work.


Best-Fit Companies Fast-shipping product companies with repeating contracts and commercial legal needs, like Series A AI startups where model changes cascade through multiple customer-facing documents.


What It Replaces Provides startup-stage companies the benefits of in-house counsel—immediate availability, business context, proactive issue prevention—before they can support that headcount.


Not Suitable For Bet-the-company litigation, novel regulatory disputes, or IPOs; forward deployment addresses the operating layer where many small decisions set company pace.


Assessment Questions Track contract turnaround time, check if sales reps have written guidance for unfamiliar terms, and measure how long contracts lag behind product changes to identify need.


FAQs


### How is a forward-deployed attorney different from outside counsel?


A forward-deployed attorney works inside the client's Slack workspace and daily operations, reviewing the same transactions as sales leaders and anticipating issues before they arise. Outside counsel typically works on discrete matters with defined scope, through email and formal engagements, and is too distant to proactively monitor product roadmaps or deal flow.


### Why does forward deployment require fixed-fee pricing?


Hourly billing penalizes the proactive work that makes companies faster—reading product specifications, building playbooks that eliminate future questions, and being available for brief queries. Fixed fees align incentives so the lawyer benefits from creating systems that save time rather than losing revenue when questions decrease.


### What types of companies benefit most from forward-deployed attorneys?


Companies that ship products quickly, have repeatable contracts with recurring customer objections, and face mostly commercial legal questions rather than specialized litigation or regulatory matters. An AI company at the Series A stage is a typical fit, where product changes cascade through multiple customer-facing legal documents.


### What kinds of legal work are not suited to forward deployment?


Bet-the-company litigation, novel regulatory disputes, and initial public offerings require specialized expertise that forward deployment does not address. Forward deployment is designed for the operating layer of a business—the many small decisions each year that collectively determine the company's pace.


### How can leadership tell if they need a forward-deployed attorney?


Ask three questions: How long does a customer agreement take from first redline to signature, and does anyone track this? Can sales representatives find written answers to unfamiliar terms without opening a ticket? After a product change, how long until contracts reflect it? If the answers reveal no tracking, no written guidance, and lagging contracts, the core problem is distance, not counsel quality.
